sources.document_name: AI fictional teaching passage: a curator's account
sources.text: This passage and all its people, places and events are fictional, written by an AI assistant for a teaching exercise. The curator of the imagined North Quay community archive writes: We finally opened the exhibition together. Volunteers carried boxes from their homes, and children stopped before the wall of photographs. We chose captions short enough to read in a crowded room. The opening felt like a beginning, not a finished history. The passage is narrated by someone responsible for the exhibition. It does not identify who selected the photographs, list rejected contributions, or report every visitor's reaction.

sources.document_name: AI fictional teaching passage: a volunteer's account
sources.text: This is an AI-authored fictional companion passage, not a real interview or archival quotation. A volunteer from the same imagined exhibition writes: I recognized my father's coat in a photograph, though the caption named only the factory. I was glad that someone had kept the picture. When the curator thanked us, I applauded, but I kept the letter I had brought inside my bag. Perhaps there would be another occasion to show it. The narrator reports gratitude and hesitation but does not state why the letter was withheld, whether anybody rejected it, or what it contained.

sources.document_name: AI-authored teaching note: perspective and interpretive limits
sources.text: A first-person account gives access to a situated viewpoint, not automatic knowledge of every participant's motives. Distinguish a narrator's explicit statement from an inference based on an image, omission or contrast. The curator's collective we can be read as an aspiration to shared ownership or as a phrase that leaves differences within the group unstated. The volunteer's applause and unopened letter can support readings of tentative belonging, unresolved exclusion, or a mixture, but the text does not establish censorship or identify the letter's contents. A defensible interpretation compares details from both passages, acknowledges a plausible competing reading, and explains the limits of its claim. Different interpretations can meet these standards without using identical wording or agreeing on a single hidden intention.

sections.heading: Two fictional accounts of the same opening
sections.text: Both passages are AI-authored fictional teaching texts about an imagined North Quay community archive exhibition; they are not real interviews or archival quotations. The curator's account reports that 'We finally opened the exhibition together,' that volunteers carried boxes from their homes and children stopped before the wall of photographs, and that captions were chosen 'short enough to read in a crowded room.' It ends with the judgement that 'The opening felt like a beginning, not a finished history.' This account does not identify who selected the photographs, does not list rejected contributions, and does not report every visitor's reaction. The volunteer's account reports, 'I recognized my father's coat in a photograph, though the caption named only the factory,' adds 'I was glad that someone had kept the picture,' reports applauding when the curator thanked the volunteers, and then notes, 'I kept the letter I had brought inside my bag,' with the thought 'Perhaps there would be another occasion to show it.' The volunteer does not state why the letter was withheld, whether anyone rejected it, or what it contained.

sections.text: The teaching note supplies the interpretive rules for this task. A first-person account gives access to a situated viewpoint, not automatic knowledge of every participant's motives. Readers should distinguish a narrator's explicit statement from an inference based on an image, an omission, or a contrast. The curator's collective 'we' can be read as an aspiration to shared ownership or as a phrase that leaves differences within the group unstated. The volunteer's applause together with the unopened letter can support readings of tentative belonging, unresolved exclusion, or a mixture of the two. The note states that the text does not establish censorship and does not identify the letter's contents. A defensible interpretation compares details from both passages, acknowledges a plausible competing reading, and explains the limits of its own claim; different interpretations may meet these standards without using identical wording or agreeing on one hidden intention.

questions.focus: Compare curator and volunteer perspectives in a fictional archive exhibition account.
questions.learning_goal: Interpret the curator's and volunteer's competing accounts of a fictional archive exhibition by comparing specific details, distinguishing explicit statements from inferences, and defending a limited reading against one plausible counterreading.

sections.heading: Two fictional accounts of the same opening
sections.text: Both passages are AI-authored fictional teaching texts about an imagined North Quay community archive exhibition; they are not real interviews or archival quotations. The curator's account reports that 'We finally opened the exhibition together,' that volunteers carried boxes from their homes and children stopped before the wall of photographs, and that captions were chosen 'short enough to read in a crowded room.' It ends with the judgement that 'The opening felt like a beginning, not a finished history.' This account does not identify who selected the photographs, does not list rejected contributions, and does not report every visitor's reaction. The volunteer's account reports, 'I recognized my father's coat in a photograph, though the caption named only the factory,' adds 'I was glad that someone had kept the picture,' reports applauding when the curator thanked the volunteers, and then notes, 'I kept the letter I had brought inside my bag,' with the thought 'Perhaps there would be another occasion to show it.' The volunteer does not state why the letter was withheld, whether anyone rejected it, or what it contained.

sections.heading: Method note: situated viewpoints and interpretive limits
sections.text: The teaching note supplies the interpretive rules for this task. A first-person account gives access to a situated viewpoint, not automatic knowledge of every participant's motives. Readers should distinguish a narrator's explicit statement from an inference based on an image, an omission, or a contrast. The curator's collective 'we' can be read as an aspiration to shared ownership or as a phrase that leaves differences within the group unstated. The volunteer's applause together with the unopened letter can support readings of tentative belonging, unresolved exclusion, or a mixture of the two. The note states that the text does not establish censorship and does not identify the letter's contents. A defensible interpretation compares details from both passages, acknowledges a plausible competing reading, and explains the limits of its own claim; different interpretations may meet these standards without using identical wording or agreeing on one hidden intention.

expected_steps: Explain that each account is a situated viewpoint with no access to all participants' motives (r1).
Cite at least one specific detail from each passage and use it as evidence (r2).
Contrast what the passages explicitly state with what they omit, naming one alignment and one gap (r3).
Present a defensible reading of shared ownership or belonging supported by both passages (r4).
State a plausible competing reading and defend the chosen reading within textual limits (r5).
Mark censorship, rejection, letter contents and general visitor reactions as unestablished (r6).

questions.stem:
Read the two AI-authored fictional passages in Section 1 and the method note in Section 2. In roughly 250-350 words, write a short answer that completes all six of the following tasks, labelling your parts so the tasks are visible.

(r1) Explain what each first-person narrator can and cannot know, given that each account offers a situated viewpoint rather than access to every participant's motives.

(r2) Cite at least one specific detail from the curator's account (for example, the collective 'we' or the short captions) and at least one from the volunteer's account (for example, the father's coat, the applause, or the letter kept in the bag), and use each as evidence rather than decoration.

(r3) Compare what the two accounts explicitly state with what they omit: identify at least one point where they align and at least one gap they leave open.

(r4) Offer a defensible reading of shared ownership or belonging that draws on both passages.

(r5) State one plausible competing reading of the same evidence, then explain why your reading remains supportable given the limits of the text.

(r6) Keep every claim within what the fictional passages establish. Do not assert that the letter was rejected, that anyone was censored, what the letter contained, or how visitors generally reacted; if you raise such a possibility, mark it explicitly as speculation and say why the text cannot settle it.

Your answer is judged on how well it handles these constraints, not on agreeing with a single hidden intention.
questions.answer:
A defensible response (other readings meeting the same criteria are also acceptable).

(r1) Situated viewpoints. Each narrator reports only one position in the opening. The curator can describe the planning and the event as experienced from the organising side, but cannot report other participants' motives, and the passage does not claim to. The volunteer can report a personal memory and a personal hesitation, but not the curator's reasons or anyone else's private response.

(r2) Evidence. From the curator: 'We finally opened the exhibition together' and captions 'short enough to read in a crowded room.' From the volunteer: 'I recognized my father's coat in a photograph, though the caption named only the factory' and 'I applauded, but I kept the letter I had brought inside my bag.'

(r3) Alignment and gap. Both accounts register a genuine shared occasion: the curator's 'together' and 'beginning' answer to the volunteer's applause and gladness 'that someone had kept the picture.' The gap is that the curator's 'we' speaks for a group without saying who within it felt fully included, while the volunteer both joins the applause and holds something back, without explaining why.

(r4) Defensible reading. Read together, the texts support belonging as real but unfinished: the exhibition creates a shared occasion and preserves at least one family trace (the father's coat), while the captions compress ('named only the factory') and the unopened letter marks a contribution not yet placed. Shared ownership is an aspiration in progress, not a settled fact.

(r5) Competing reading. One could read the withheld letter as evidence of exclusion, making the 'we' a claim the volunteer cannot share. That is plausible but overreaches: the volunteer reports applause and gladness about the kept photograph, and reports hesitation rather than refusal; the method note states the text does not establish censorship. The unfinished-belonging reading accommodates both the applause and the withheld letter without inventing a cause.

(r6) Limits. Neither passage says who selected the photographs, what the letter contained, whether it was rejected, how visitors generally reacted, or what any narrator intended beyond what is stated; such claims must be dropped or clearly marked as speculation.
questions.explanation: A strong answer works through the six labelled tasks rather than summarising the passages. It states that each first-person account is a situated viewpoint (r1), quotes concrete details from both passages as evidence (r2), sets explicit statements against omissions and names one alignment and one gap (r3), proposes a reading of shared ownership or belonging that both passages can carry (r4), gives a genuine competing reading and explains why the first reading survives it (r5), and disciplines its own claims, treating censorship, rejection, the letter's contents, and general visitor reactions as unestablished (r6). Readings of 'tentative belonging', 'unresolved exclusion', or a mixture can all qualify if they meet these conditions; there is no single required hidden intention.
questions.difficulty_reason: The task cannot be completed by restating a definition. It requires integrating two passages with an interpretive method note, selecting and quoting evidence from both, distinguishing explicit statement from inference, producing an interpretation and then a genuine counter-reading, and actively suppressing several tempting claims (censorship, rejection, letter contents, visitor reactions) that the passages do not support. The constraints operate simultaneously, so a response that satisfies the interpretive demand but violates the evidential limits fails.
